name: Apache Parquet
summary: The standard columnar file format for analytics: each column stored and compressed on its own, with statistics that let engines skip data.
intro: A Parquet file splits its rows into row groups. Inside each row group, every column is stored as its own column chunk, broken into pages. Values of one type sit next to each other, so dictionary and run-length encodings plus a codec such as Snappy or ZSTD shrink them well. The footer comes last, so a writer can produce the file in one pass, and it holds the schema and min/max statistics for every column chunk.

A reader fetches the footer first, then reads only the column chunks a query names and skips row groups whose statistics rule out a match. Nested data (structs, lists, maps) is flattened into plain columns with the record shredding algorithm from Google’s Dremel paper. Twitter and Cloudera started Parquet in 2013. It’s now an Apache project and the default data file format under table formats such as Iceberg and Delta Lake.
strengths: Read by practically every engine and library, including Spark, Trino, DuckDB, BigQuery, Athena and pandas
Queries read only the columns and row groups they need, often a small fraction of the file
Compresses well, because each column gets its own encoding and compression codec
The schema, including nested types, travels inside the file
limits: A file can’t be edited in place: changing one row means rewriting the file, which is why table formats exist
Built for batches; writing one event at a time is slow and produces tiny files
Thousands of small files scan slowly; the format’s own guidance is large row groups of 512 MB to 1 GB
A folder of Parquet files isn’t a table: no transactions, no shared schema, no record of which files belong

story: Google’s 2010 Dremel paper showed that storing nested records column by column let it aggregate trillion-row tables in seconds. Hadoop users wanted the same for their files on HDFS, and by early 2013 several columnar formats were competing, including Doug Cutting’s Trevni and ORC, which Hortonworks and Facebook built to speed up Hive. One Hadoop user replied to the next announcement: “Do we really need 3 columnar formats?”

That announcement, on 12 March 2013, introduced Parquet as a joint project between Twitter and Cloudera engineers. Julien Le Dem started it at Twitter together with Cloudera’s Impala team, and Criteo engineers signed up to build the Hive support. The goal was to make compressed columnar storage “available to any project in the Hadoop ecosystem, regardless of the choice of data processing framework, data model, or programming language.” Twitter began converting its major data sources to save on storage and deserialization. Le Dem later wrote that the name was picked to evoke “the bottom layer of a database with an interesting layout.”

Version 1.0 shipped in July 2013. Parquet entered the Apache Incubator in May 2014 and became a top-level project in April 2015. It went on to become the default data file under almost every lake engine and table format.

choices.choice: Dremel’s repetition and definition levels for nested data
choices.why: Hadoop data was often nested objects (the first release converted Thrift objects directly). Storing each leaf field as a column plus small level numbers keeps the nesting without flattening field names.

choices.choice: Compression per column, separate from encoding
choices.why: Each column picks its own codec, and encodings are kept apart from compression so engines can work on encoded values without paying to decode them.

choices.choice: A neutral format with no favourite engine
choices.why: The founders said they were “not interested in playing favorites” and shipped building blocks for Pig, Hive, Impala, Thrift and Avro, so no single framework owned the format.
